{{Short description|Scheme in algebraic geometry}}
{{for|normal cones in real vector spaces|convex cone}}
In [[algebraic geometry]], the '''normal cone''' of a subscheme of a [[scheme (mathematics)|scheme]] is a scheme analogous to the [[normal bundle]] or [[tubular neighborhood]] in [[differential geometry]].

==Definition==

The normal cone {{math|C<sub>''X''</sub>''Y''}} or <math>C_{X/Y}</math> of an embedding {{math|''i'': ''X'' &rarr; ''Y''}}, defined by some [[sheaf of ideals]] ''I'', is defined as the [[relative Spec]]
<math display="block"> \operatorname{Spec}_X \left(\bigoplus_{n = 0}^{\infty} I^n / I^{n+1}\right).</math>

When the embedding ''i'' is [[regular embedding|regular]] the normal cone is the normal bundle, the [[vector bundle]] on ''X'' corresponding to the dual of the sheaf {{math|''I''/''I''<sup>2</sup>}}.

If ''X'' is a point, then the normal cone and the normal bundle to it are also called the [[tangent cone]] and the [[tangent space]] ([[Zariski tangent space]]) to the point. When ''Y'' = Spec ''R'' is affine, the definition means that the normal cone to ''X'' = Spec ''R''/''I'' is the Spec of the [[associated graded ring]] of ''R'' with respect to ''I''.

If ''Y'' is the product ''X'' × ''X'' and the embedding ''i'' is the [[diagonal embedding]], then the normal bundle to ''X'' in ''Y'' is the [[tangent bundle]] to ''X''.

The normal cone (or rather its projective cousin) appears as a result of [[blowing up|blow-up]]. Precisely, let
<math display="block">\pi: \operatorname{Bl}_X Y = \operatorname{Proj}_Y \left(\bigoplus_{n=0}^{\infty} I^n\right) \to Y</math>
be the blow-up of ''Y'' along ''X''. Then, by definition, the [[exceptional divisor]] is the pre-image <math>E = \pi^{-1}(X)</math>; which is the [[cone (algebraic geometry)|projective cone]] of <math display="inline">\bigoplus_0^{\infty} I^n \otimes_{\mathcal{O}_Y} \mathcal{O}_X = \bigoplus_0^{\infty} I^n/I^{n+1}</math>. Thus,
<math display="block">E = \mathbb{P}(C_X Y).</math>

The global sections of the normal bundle classify [[embedded infinitesimal deformation]]s of ''Y'' in ''X''; there is a natural [[bijection]] between the set of closed subschemes of {{math|''Y'' ×<sub>''k''</sub> ''D''}}, [[flat morphism|flat]] over the ring ''D'' of [[Dual_number#Generalizations|dual numbers]] and having ''X'' as the special fiber, and ''H''<sup>0</sup>(''X'', ''N''<sub>''X''</sub> ''Y'').{{sfn|Hartshorne|1977|page=Ch. III, Exercise 9.7.}}

== Properties ==

=== Compositions of regular embeddings ===
If <math>i: X \hookrightarrow Y, \, j: Y \hookrightarrow Z</math> are [[regular embedding|regular embeddings]], then <math>j \circ i</math> is a regular embedding and there is a natural [[exact sequence]] of vector bundles on ''X'':{{sfn|Fulton|1998|page=Appendix B.7.4.}}
<math display="block">0\to N_{X/Y} \to N_{X/Z} \to i^* N_{Y/Z} \to 0.</math>

If <math>Y_i \hookrightarrow X</math> are regular embeddings of codimensions <math>c_i</math> and if <math display="inline">W := \bigcap_i Y_i \hookrightarrow X</math> is a regular embedding of codimension <math display="block">\sum c_i</math> then{{sfn|Fulton|1998|page=Appendix B.7.4.}}
<math display="block">N_{W/X} = \bigoplus_i N_{Y_i/X}|_W.</math>
In particular, if <math>X \to S</math> is a [[smooth morphism]], then the normal bundle to the [[diagonal embedding]] <math display="block">\Delta: X \hookrightarrow X \times_S \cdots \times_S X</math> (''r''-fold) is the direct sum of {{math|''r'' − 1}} copies of the [[relative tangent bundle]] <math>T_{X/S}</math>.

If <math>X \hookrightarrow Y</math> is a [[closed immersion]] and if <math>Y' \to Y</math> is a flat morphism such that <math>X' = X \times_Y Y'</math>, then{{sfn|Fulton|1998|page=The first part of the proof of Theorem 6.5.}}{{citation needed|date=August 2020}}<!-- Fulton only considers the case of a vector bundle. -->
<math display="block">C_{X'/Y'} = C_{X/Y} \times_X X'.</math>

If <math>X \to S</math> is a [[smooth morphism]] and <math>X \hookrightarrow Y</math> is a regular embedding, then there is a natural exact sequence of vector bundles on ''X'':{{sfn|Fulton|1998|page=Appendix B 7.1.}}
<math display="block">0 \to T_{X/S} \to T_{Y/S}|_X \to N_{X/Y} \to 0</math>
(which is a special case of an exact sequence for [[cotangent sheaf|cotangent sheaves]]).

=== Cartesian square ===
For a Cartesian square of schemes <math display="block">\begin{matrix}
X' & \to & Y' \\
\downarrow & & \downarrow \\
X & \to & Y
\end{matrix}</math> with <math>f:X' \to X</math> the vertical map, there is a closed embedding <math display="block"> C_{X'/Y'} \hookrightarrow f^*C_{X/Y}</math> of normal cones.

=== Dimension of components ===
Let <math>X</math> be a scheme of finite type over a field and <math>W \subset X</math> a closed subscheme. If <math>X</math> is of {{nowrap|[[pure dimension]] ''r''}}; i.e., every irreducible component has dimension ''r'', then <math>C_{W/X}</math> is also of pure dimension ''r''.{{sfn|Fulton|1998|page=Appendix B. 6.6.}} (This can be seen as a consequence of [[#Deformation to the normal cone]].) This property is a key to an application in [[intersection theory]]: given a pair of closed subschemes <math>V, X</math> in some ambient space, while the [[scheme-theoretic intersection]] <math>V \cap X</math> has irreducible components of various dimensions, depending delicately on the positions of <math>V, X</math>, the normal cone to <math>V \cap X</math> is of pure dimension.

== Examples ==
Let <math>D \hookrightarrow X</math> be an effective [[Cartier divisor]]. Then the normal bundle to it (or equivalently the normal cone to it) is{{sfn|Fulton|1998|page=Appendix B.6.2.}} <math display="block">N_{D/X} = \mathcal{O}_D(D) := \mathcal{O}_X(D)|_D.</math>

===Non-regular embedding===
Consider the non-regular embedding<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal| last1=Battistella|first1=Luca| last2=Carocci|first2=Francesca| last3=Manolache|first3=Cristina| date=2020-04-09| title=Virtual classes for the working mathematician| journal=Symmetry, Integrability and Geometry: Methods and Applications| doi=10.3842/SIGMA.2020.026|arxiv=1804.06048 | doi-access=free}}</ref>{{rp|pp=4-5}}
<math display="block">X = \text{Spec}\left( \frac{\mathbb{C}[x,y,z]}{(xz,yz)}\right) \to \mathbb{A}^3</math>
then, we can compute the normal cone by first observing
<math display="block">\begin{align}
I &= (xz, yz) \\
I^2 &= (x^2z^2, xyz^2, y^2z^2) \\
\end{align}</math>
If we make the auxiliary variables <math>a = xz</math> and <math>b = yz</math>  we get the relation
<math display="block">ya - xb = 0.</math>
We can use this to give a presentation of the normal cone as the relative spectrum
<math display="block"> C_X \mathbb{A}^3 = \text{Spec}_X \left( \frac{\mathcal{O}_X[a,b]}{(ya-xb)} \right)</math>
Since <math>\mathbb{A}^3</math> is affine, we can just write out the relative spectrum as the affine scheme <math display="block">C_X \mathbb{A}^3 = \text{Spec}\left( \frac{\mathbb{C}[x,y,z][a,b]}{(xz,yz,ya-xb)} \right)</math> giving us the normal cone.

==== Geometry of this normal cone ====
The normal cone's geometry can be further explored by looking at the fibers for various closed points of <math>X</math>. Note that geometrically <math>X</math> is the union of the <math>xy</math>-plane <math>H</math> with the <math>z</math>-axis <math>L</math>, <math display="block">X = H \cup L</math> so the points of interest are smooth points on the plane, smooth points on the axis, and the point on their intersection. Any smooth point on the plane is given by a map <math display="block">\begin{matrix}
x \mapsto z_1 & y \mapsto z_2 & z \mapsto 0  
\end{matrix}</math> for <math>z_1,z_2 \in \mathbb{C}</math> and either <math>z_1 \neq 0</math> or <math>z_2\neq 0</math>. Since it is arbitrary which point we take, for convenience let us assume <math>z_1 \neq 0, z_2 = 0</math>. Hence the fiber of <math>C_X\mathbb{A}^3</math> at the point <math>p=(z_1,0,0)</math> is isomorphic to <math display="block">C_X \mathbb{A}^3 |_p \cong \frac{\mathbb{C}[a,b]}{(z_1b)} \cong \mathbb{C}[a]</math> giving the normal cone as a one dimensional line, as expected. For a point <math>q</math> on the axis, this is given by a map <math display="block">\begin{matrix}
x \mapsto 0 & y \mapsto 0 & z \mapsto z_3  
\end{matrix}</math> hence the fiber at the point <math>q = (0,0,z_3)</math> is <math display="block">C_X \mathbb{A}^3 |_q \cong \frac{\mathbb{C}[a,b]}{(0)} \cong \mathbb{C}[a,b]</math> which gives a plane. At the origin <math>r = (0,0,0)</math>, the normal cone over that point is again isomorphic to <math>\mathbb{C}[a,b]</math>.

=== Nodal cubic ===
For the nodal cubic curve <math>Y</math> given by the polynomial <math>y^2 + x^2(x-1)</math> over <math>\mathbb{C}</math>, and <math>X</math> the point at the node, the cone has the isomorphism <math display="block">C_{X/Y} \cong \text{Spec}\left(\mathbb{C}[x,y]/\left(y^2-x^2\right)\right)</math> showing the normal cone has more components than the scheme it lies over.

==Deformation to the normal cone==
<!-- Should discuss how this is a flat deformation, hence the name https://mathoverflow.net/questions/56897/deformation-to-the-normal-cone -->Suppose <math>i : X \to Y</math> is an embedding. This can be deformed to the embedding of <math>X</math> inside the normal cone <math>C_{X/Y}</math> (as the zero section) in the following sense:<ref name=":0" />{{rp|6}} there is a flat family <math display="block">\pi : M^o_{X/Y} \to \mathbb{P}^1</math> with generic fiber <math>Y</math> and special fiber <math>C_{X/Y}</math> such that there exists a family of closed embeddings <math display="block">X \times \mathbb{P}^1 \hookrightarrow M^o_{X/Y}</math> over <math>\mathbb{P}^1</math> such that

# Over any point <math>t \in \mathbb{P}^1-\{0\}</math> the associated embeddings are an embedding <math>X\times\{t\} \hookrightarrow Y</math>
# The fiber over <math>0 \in \mathbb{P}^1</math> is the embedding of <math>X \hookrightarrow C_{X/Y}</math> given by the zero section.

This construction defines a tool analogous to [[differential topology]] where non-transverse intersections are performed in a tubular neighborhood of the intersection. Now, the intersection of <math>X</math> with a cycle <math>Z</math> in <math>Y</math> can be given as the pushforward of an intersection of <math>X</math> with the pullback of <math>Z</math> in <math>C_{X/Y}</math>.

=== Construction ===
One application of this is to define intersection products in the [[Chow ring]]. Suppose that ''X'' and ''V'' are closed subschemes of ''Y'' with intersection ''W'', and we wish to define the intersection product of ''X'' and ''V'' in the Chow ring of ''Y''. Deformation to the normal cone in this case means that we replace the embeddings of ''X'' and ''W'' in ''Y'' and ''V'' by their normal cones ''C''<sub>''Y''</sub>(''X'') and ''C''<sub>''W''</sub>(''V''), so that we want to find the product of ''X'' and ''C''<sub>''W''</sub>''V'' in ''C''<sub>''X''</sub>''Y''.
This can be much easier: for example, if ''X'' is [[regularly embedded]] in ''Y'' then its normal cone is a vector bundle, so we are reduced to the problem of finding the intersection product of a subscheme ''C''<sub>''W''</sub>''V'' of a vector bundle ''C''<sub>''X''</sub>''Y'' with the zero section ''X''. However this intersection product is just given by applying the Gysin isomorphism to ''C''<sub>''W''</sub>''V''.

Concretely, the deformation to the normal cone can be constructed by means of blowup. Precisely, let
<math display="block">\pi: M \to Y \times \mathbb{P}^1</math>
be the blow-up of <math>Y \times \mathbb{P}^1</math> along <math>X \times 0</math>. The exceptional divisor is <math>\overline{C_X Y} = \mathbb{P}(C_X Y \oplus 1)</math>, the projective completion of the normal cone; for the notation used here see {{slink|Cone (algebraic geometry)#Properties}}. The normal cone <math>C_X Y</math> is an open subscheme of <math>\overline{C_X Y}</math> and <math>X</math> is embedded as a zero-section into <math>C_X Y</math>.

Now, we note:
#The map <math>\rho: M \to \mathbb{P}^1</math>, the <math>\pi</math> followed by projection, is flat.
#There is an induced closed embedding <math display="block">\widetilde{i}: X \times \mathbb{P}^1 \hookrightarrow M</math> that is a morphism over <math>\mathbb{P}^1</math>.
#''M'' is trivial away from zero; i.e., <math>\rho^{-1}(\mathbb{P}^1 - 0)= Y \times (\mathbb{P}^1 - 0)</math> and <math>\widetilde{i}</math> restricts to the trivial embedding <math display="block">X \times (\mathbb{P}^1 - 0) \hookrightarrow Y \times (\mathbb{P}^1 - 0).</math>
# <math>\rho^{-1}(0)</math> as the divisor is the sum <math display="block"> \overline{C_X Y} + \widetilde{Y}</math> where <math>\widetilde{Y}</math> is the blow-up of ''Y'' along ''X'' and is viewed as an effective Cartier divisor.
#As divisors <math>\overline{C_X Y}</math> and <math> \widetilde{Y}</math> intersect at <math>\mathbb{P}(C)</math>, where <math>\mathbb{P}(C)</math> sits at infinity in <math>\overline{C_X Y}</math>.
Item 1 is clear (check torsion-free-ness). In general, given <math>X \subset Y</math>, we have <math>\operatorname{Bl}_V X \subset \operatorname{Bl}_V Y</math>. Since <math>X \times 0</math> is already an effective Cartier divisor on <math>X \times \mathbb{P}^1</math>, we get
<math display="block">X \times \mathbb{P}^1 = \operatorname{Bl}_{X \times 0} X \times \mathbb{P}^1 \hookrightarrow M,</math>
yielding <math>\widetilde{i}</math>. Item 3 follows from the fact the blowdown map π is an isomorphism away from the center <math>X \times 0</math>. The last two items are seen from explicit local computation. [[Q.E.D.]]

Now, the last item in the previous paragraph implies that the image of <math>X \times 0</math> in ''M'' does not intersect <math>\widetilde{Y}</math>. Thus, one gets the deformation of ''i'' to the zero-section embedding of ''X'' into the normal cone.

== Intrinsic normal cone ==

=== Intrinsic normal bundle ===
Let <math>X</math> be a [[Deligne–Mumford stack]] locally of finite type over a field <math>k</math>. If <math>\textbf{L}_X</math> denotes the [[cotangent complex]] of ''X'' relative to <math>k</math>, then the '''intrinsic normal bundle'''<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal| last1=Behrend|first1=K.| last2=Fantechi|first2=B.| date=1997-03-19| title=The intrinsic normal cone| journal=Inventiones Mathematicae| volume=128| issue=1|pages=45–88| doi=10.1007/s002220050136|arxiv=alg-geom/9601010 |s2cid=18533009 | issn=0020-9910}}</ref>{{rp|27}} to <math>X</math> is the [[quotient stack]] <math display="block">\mathfrak{N}_X := h^1 / h^0(\textbf{L}_{X, \text{fppf}}^{\vee})</math> which is the stack of fppf <math>\textbf{L}_X^{\vee, 0}</math>-[[torsor (algebraic geometry)|torsors]] on <math>\textbf{L}_X^{\vee, 1}</math>. A concrete interpretation of this stack quotient can be given by looking at its behavior locally in the étale topos of the stack <math>X</math>.

==== Properties of intrinsic normal bundle ====
More concretely, suppose there is an étale morphism <math>U \to X</math> from an affine finite-type <math>k</math>-scheme <math>U</math> together with a locally closed immersion <math>f: U \to M</math> into a smooth affine finite-type <math>k</math>-scheme <math>M</math>. Then one can show <math display="block">\mathfrak{N}_X |_U = [N_{U/M}/f^* T_M]</math> meaning we can understand the intrinsic normal bundle as a stacky incarnation for the failure of the normal sequence <math display="block">\mathcal{T}_U \to \mathcal{T}_M |_U \to \mathcal{N}_{U/M}</math> to be exact on the right hand side. Moreover, for special cases discussed below, we are now considering the quotient as a continuation of the previous sequence as a triangle in some [[triangulated category]]. This is because the local stack quotient <math>[N_{U/M}/f^* T_M]</math> can be interpreted as <math display="block">B \mathcal{T}_U = \mathcal{T}_U[+1]</math> in certain cases.

=== Normal cone ===
The '''intrinsic normal cone''' to <math>X</math>, denoted as <math>\mathfrak{C}_X</math>,<ref name=":1" />{{rp|29}} is then defined by replacing the normal bundle <math>N_{U/M}</math> with the normal cone <math>C_{U/M}</math>; i.e.,
<math display="block">\mathfrak{C}_X|_U = [C_{U/M} / f^* T_M].</math>

'''Example''': One has that <math>X</math> is a local complete intersection if and only if <math>\mathfrak{C}_X = \mathfrak{N}_X</math>. In particular, if <math>X</math> is [[smooth stack|smooth]], then <math>\mathfrak{C}_X = \mathfrak{N}_X = B T_X</math> is the [[classifying stack]] of the tangent bundle <math>T_X</math>, which is a commutative [[group scheme]] over <math>X</math>.

More generally, let <math>X \to Y</math> is a Deligne-Mumford Type (DM-type) morphism of Artin Stacks which is locally of finite type. Then <math>\mathfrak{C}_{X/Y} \subseteq \mathfrak{N}_{X/Y}</math> is characterised as the closed substack such that, for any étale map <math>U \to X</math> for which <math>U \to X \to Y</math> factors through some smooth map <math>M \to Y</math> (e.g., <math>\mathbb{A}_Y^n \to Y</math>), the pullback is:
<math display="block">\mathfrak{C}_{X/Y}|_U = [C_{U/M} / T_{M/Y}|_U].</math>
